name: Leonard 'Len' Garrity
languages: Enough French from the Boston police courts to know when he is being insulted
equipment: Heavy coat: a grey chesterfield overcoat with a velvet collar gone bald, bought in better days, over a brown three-piece suit
Service revolver (a .38 Police Positive he got a permit for after a story about the North End went wrong), 6 loaded, in a shoulder holster he finds uncomfortable
Walking stick, malacca with a silver knob, which he carries because a man with a stick is taken for a gentleman and a man with a notebook is taken for a reporter

A Merrymeeting Life & Casualty Company claim file on three Carrow Island policies: Esther Thurlow, $3,000, beneficiary her brother Dr. N. Thurlow of Bangor; Clyde Tibbetts, $2,000, beneficiary Verna Tibbetts, taken out in May 1924; Jotham Wyman, $1,000, beneficiary Ellery Wyman
A folding Kodak camera, two rolls of film and a flash lamp
A steel tape measure, a pocket magnifier, a pair of field glasses and a fountain pen that leaks
A notebook in Pitman shorthand, half full
A pocket flask of rye, technically illegal, for interviewing fishermen
A Merrymeeting Life business card case and a letter of authority from the company's claims department in Bath
features: Seen It in a Book (Educated origin: once per long rest, recalls one true and useful fact of history, science, law or a book without a check; advantage on Research checks in a library, archive or registry; reads old handwriting, Latin inscriptions and legal language without a check)

There's an Explanation (Skeptic: once per short rest, when he fails a fear check, he names a rational cause aloud, a draught, a prankster, a trick of the light, and the failure becomes a success with no Dread; it does not have to be true, and if it is the GM says so. Advantage on Investigation checks to find the mechanism behind something that is not supernatural; after 10 minutes searching a room, the GM tells him whether any part of what is happening in it is a person's doing)

Careful Notes (Skeptic: once per short rest, after 10 minutes examining a scene, he asks 'What here has been moved?', 'Who was here most recently?' or 'What here does not fit?' and gets a true answer; a clue, never a creature's rule outright)

Calm Explanation (Skeptic, 2nd level: as an action, once per long rest, he explains a frightening phenomenon to allies who can hear him; until the end of the scene they have advantage on fear checks against that one horror)

Discipline: Debunker (Skeptic, 3rd level: advantage on checks to see through Deception and stage trickery, and when a person or creature tries to frighten him with something that is not supernatural, he automatically succeeds on the fear check)

The Morgue and the Wire (Reporter background: nine years on Boston papers; he can get into any newspaper's back files with the staff's help, reads a court docket, a coroner's report and a police blotter, and finds the town's gossip in any place with a paper; and a story with his name on it tells everyone who has been asking)

personality.traits: I talk like a newspaper: short, fast and with a punchline. Everybody lies to an insurance man; it's practically a sacrament, and I don't hold it against them. I write everything down, including what people did with their hands while they told me.
personality.ideals: There is always an explanation, and it is nearly always money. The rest of the time it is love, which is worse. If a man tells you his house is haunted, look at the mortgage.
personality.bonds: Merrymeeting Life, which pays me forty dollars a week and doesn't ask how. My mother in Dorchester, who lights a candle for me every Sunday and is the only person who knows I go with her sometimes. The truth, which I used to sell by the column inch and now sell by the claim.
personality.flaws: I am sure. I was sure in 1919 when I exposed Professor Septimus Orr, the Back Bay spirit medium, as a fraud with wires and a cheesecloth ghost, and I was right, and I have been sure ever since. I would rather be wrong in a way I can explain than right in a way I can't.

appearance: A lean, sharp-faced man of forty with thinning sandy hair under a grey fedora, a clipped moustache, quick pale blue eyes, a nose that has been broken once by a ward heeler, and ink-stained cuffs. Chesterfield coat, a suit that has been good, a silver-knobbed stick, and the habit of looking at the floor of every room before he looks at the people in it.
backstory: Leonard Garrity grew up over his father's barbershop in Dorchester and talked his way onto the Boston Post at seventeen as a copy runner. By twenty-five he was a police reporter, and by thirty he was the man the Post sent when somebody wanted a scandal: crooked aldermen, fake charities, and in 1919 the famous Professor Septimus Orr of Commonwealth Avenue, whose seances raised the dead for grieving mothers at twenty dollars a sitting, until Len Garrity hid in a cupboard with a flash camera and photographed the Professor's assistant in a cheesecloth veil. In 1921 a story about a city contractor that he could not prove cost the Post a libel suit and cost Len his job, and Merrymeeting Life & Casualty of Bath, which had read his stories, hired him to investigate doubtful claims. He has found arson, fake drownings, a man who sold his own corpse twice and a widow who was not one. Now Merrymeeting has three claims from one small island in six weeks, all drownings, no bodies, and the company's claims manager, who reads the Rockland paper, says the islanders blame a ghost bell. Len thinks it is rum-runners or fraud or both. He has noticed that one of the beneficiaries, Dr. Nathan Thurlow, is booked on the same mail boat. (Hook: the ghost story is a fraud and one of the drownings is a fake. He is right about one of the three, and that is the trap.)
